description:
Peak of Eternal Light is a one-person team from Ukraine with a background in power engineering and embedded systems.

We turn lunar terrain and ephemerides into the number that actually decides a landing site: how long the darkness lasts, and whether your batteries survive it.
summary:
Peak of Eternal Light is a web application that evaluates lunar landing sites and dates by two conditions a lander depends on: sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for direct communication. Near the south pole the Sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon, so terrain up to hundreds of kilometres away controls both. For any point on the Moon and any date from 1969 to 2036, the application derives the terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation models and the positions of the Sun and Earth from NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides. From these it computes windows of illumination and Earth visibility, the time to the next sunset or Earthset, and whether a given battery survives the night. It includes the CLPS deliveries, Apollo, Chang'e, SLIM and Chandrayaan-3, compares sites and dates side by side, and shows how results change with the touchdown point. Mean illumination agrees with NASA's published maps (r = 0.995); computed sunsets match the reported ends of Chandrayaan-3, IM-1 and Blue Ghost 1 operations. CLPS and Artemis missions to the south pole are planned around these windows; the application makes the analysis available in any browser without specialist software.
Repo: https://github.com/RenatTOP/peak-of-eternal-light
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Peak of Eternal Light computes, for a point on the lunar surface and a period of time, when the Sun and Earth are above the local terrain horizon. The user selects a catalog site (candidate south polar regions, landed missions, permanently shadowed craters), a mission from the CLPS catalog, any point on the globe or polar map, or typed coordinates, and a period between 1969 and 2035. The application shows the 360° horizon with the tracks of the Sun and Earth, every window of sunlight, Earth visibility and both together, the time to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset or Earthrise, and four summary metrics: mean solar energy share, Earth visibility, simultaneous coverage and the longest night. Further functions: a power model (sun-tracking panel, battery, operating and survival loads) that reports whether and when the battery empties; a survey of landing dates over a year; side-by-side scenarios aligned by days since landing; a scan of 37 points within 5 km that shows how results depend on the touchdown point and local slope; rover traverses with a least-darkness path search over NASA mean illumination maps; 3D views lit by the computed Sun direction; five guided tours. Every view is encoded in a shareable link.

HOW IT WORKS

An offline Python pipeline processes about 80 GB of NASA data. Horizons are traced along 720 or 1440 azimuths to 300 km with nested terrain: 5 m LOLA and shape-from-shading models near catalog sites, 20–240 m LOLA polar models beyond, 59 m SLDEM2015 at landing sites off the pole, and the 474 m global LOLA grid elsewhere. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/JPL SPICE (DE440, MOON_ME frame) at 6 h steps and are interpolated in the browser with a direction error below 2·10⁻⁵°. For an arbitrary point the browser traces the near horizon itself from terrain tiles and adds a precomputed distant horizon, so any location can be analysed without a server. The visible fraction of each disc above the horizon is computed at every time step, and event times are refined to one minute.

VALIDATION

Mean illumination and Earth visibility at 229 stratified points agree with the NASA maps of Mazarico et al. (r = 0.995; bias −0.6 and +1.1 percentage points). Solar elevations at the Apollo 11 and 12 touchdowns differ from the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal by 0.05°. Computed sunsets coincide with the end of operations of Chandrayaan-3 (4 September 2023) and IM-1 (2 March 2024); at Blue Ghost 1 the Sun begins to set 7–27 minutes after the end of daylight inferred from Firefly's reports. 128 automated tests check the browser formulas against the Python reference.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Sunlight and line of sight to Earth constrain landing site and date selection, battery sizing and mission duration for CLPS and Artemis missions to the south pole. Existing products provide long-term averages or require GIS software and SPICE expertise. This application gives time-resolved answers for a specific place and date in a browser: mission planners can compare options at an early stage, and students and the public can see why polar landers depend on terrain and why missions end at sunset.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, rasterio, spiceypy), TypeScript, React, Three.js, Leaflet, Vite, Vitest; static hosting on Cloudflare Pages. No specialised hardware.

CREATIVITY

Horizons are traced in the browser, which removes the restriction to a precomputed list of sites. Near and distant terrain are treated separately, which keeps results on peaks and crater rims correct. Time is a primary axis: countdowns, the landing-date survey and scenarios aligned by days since landing. Uncertainty is shown explicitly, through 100 terrain realisations within the LOLA error (Barker et al. 2021) and the touchdown scan.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Terrain resolution near the observer, which dominates the error on ridges and rims; the finite discs of the Sun and Earth rather than their centres; time systems (UTC in the browser, TDB in SPICE); data volume for a static site (about 0.9 GB, terrain tiles loaded on demand). Limitations are stated in the application: off the pole, outside the precomputed landing sites, 474 m terrain can shift sunrise and sunset by one to two hours; slopes are underestimated; the power presets are generic rather than specific spacecraft.

USE OF AI

Parts of the code and data pipeline were written with an AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude), which was also used for literature and mission research and to interpret validation results. No data, results or images in the application are AI-generated, except for the logo, the team avatar and the mission patches, which are clearly marked as such: every number is computed by the model described above from the listed NASA products and checked by automated tests against Python references, NASA maps and mission events.
